title: The Atlantic Club and Swedish club life
summary: She describes the club, its membership, its owner Bo, and the contrast with younger clubs.

any interest to what we're doing on this tape? Is it -- I've never heard of it before. Is it an important jazz spot in Sweden?

It was at the time. When we played the first engagement there -- you know, when we had the three days -- Bo Stemhammer, who owned the club and operated the club, they had just moved in there. And they were still in the process of decorating the club.

And of course we later appeared at the Club each year for three years, one time for a two-week engagement and then two three-week engagements, but we understand that Bo Stemhammer sold the Atlantic Club. The way we got it was, it wasn't a case of not making enough money, he was making too much money and he sold the Club and right now he is operating and introducing, I suppose, performances for a club in Stockholm called the Mosebacke which is a local club and I imagine it's more or less subsidized, underwritten by the Swedish government, it's a little cultural facility there.

I was there two years ago and I went over to do a broadcast for the Swedish Broadcasting System and we were doing a Festival which occurs around Eastertime and I appeared at the Mosebacke for three days, and while I was there, Wild Bill Davis who was living in Copenhagen at the time, he was passing through, so he did one night at the Mosebacke and then -- in fact he did two nights and one of the nights I was there, Budd Johnson was on his way through on tour and I worked one night with him, but with local musicians and so the Mosebacke is where he's situated now.

The Atlantic was a very good club, so far as I was concerned. It was large, I imagine it had a capacity of about maybe 400 and the audiences were just terrific and the place was packed every night and they really loved the band, they danced and it sort of took me back to those early days when we had the Savoy Ballroom, the Roseland Ballroom where the patrons really came to dance, and they were swinging. And there were some young, Swedish couples there that really weren't into the swing, but some of the older patrons -- I found out a lot of them had visited the United States and a lot of them had gone to New Orleans for the New Orleans Jazz Festival, and a lot of them really travelled quite extensively --
I understand it was a very exclusive Club.

Well, it may have been exclusive because it may have been a little more expensive -- well, actually -- all right, so we visited some other little jazz clubs in Stockholm and most of the jazz clubs that we visited were, let's say the noncommercial type, they featured the local

musicians and they were membership clubs more or less or I imagine they got the same patrons all the time and they would have maybe a different group each night or maybe they'd have a group in for a couple of nights, but it was the same type of club that some of the early little jazz clubs. We had jazz fans that would come that were really into jazz, knowing the musicians by name. I don't think that the people who came to the Atlantic were that particular about who was who except they'd just come there to dance and enjoy the music. I mean, naturally, they would find out who the musicians were if they happened to be jazz fans; but I think the majority of the patrons came, they just came to dance and hear the music and they knew it was the world's greatest jazz band, they knew what kind of music they were going to hear and that was that. There was very little interaction between the patrons and the musicians, you know, we just played.
Wherein the other little clubs, the young people that would come, they knew -- they were up on what was the latest thing and there was a lot
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

of conversation between the musicians and patrons but I would say by comparison, the Atlantic Club was a commercial-type club and maybe a little bit more expensive than, say, the average young jazz fan would be able to afford.
Still it's extraordinary to hear any kind of jazz enterprise that was making too much money.

Well, that's the story -- Bo -- I'd say Bo might be about in his 30s, but since I've been over there the last time -- I think he got married and he had a little son and the last time I heard from him which was this year because I was supposed to go over there this year and do the broadcast again in the Festival, but I couldn't go because I was in the hospital.

I'm thinking that what he wanted to do was to have a little bit more time with the family life because that Club took up all his time, you know, when you have a large enterprise, you have a lot of people to worry about, you have to be there all the time.

I think right now he's happy -- I think he's sorry he got rid of the Atlantic Club, too, because he can't -- there's a possibility also that it became a little bit maybe unprofitable for him to try to bring a whole American band over, you know, salaries, accommodations and the trip across the Atlantic. So it seems that the thing now is like for individual musicians to go over and work with local musicians because they can afford that. And a lot of that is going on right now.
